title: Black Jack Drive-Maxx Review: 500 vs 700 vs 1000 Compared
h1: Black Jack Drive-Maxx Review (500 vs 700 vs 1000)
description: Yes, Drive-Maxx is sound: the number is the rated life (500 = 5 years, 1000 = 10). All need two coats at 350 sq ft a pail; only the 1000 goes to 45°F.
dek: What actually changes between the 500, 700 and 1000, from Black Jack's own data sheets.
quickAnswer: Yes, Drive-Maxx is a competent consumer sealer range. The number is the rated life in years: 500 = 5, 700 = 7, 1000 = 10. All three need two thin coats at about 350 sq ft per coat (300 on rough asphalt) per 4.75-gallon pail. The 500 and 700 need 55-90°F; the 1000 goes down at 45°F, recoats in 2-4 hours and takes light foot traffic in about an hour in good drying conditions. Vehicles wait at least 24 hours on all three.
intro: Black Jack Drive-Maxx is one of the most widely stocked driveway sealer ranges in North America, and the numbers on the pails raise the same questions every spring: what is the difference between the 500, 700 and 1000, is the 1000 worth the extra money, and how long does each really last.

This review is built from Black Jack's published technical data sheets and label directions (Black Jack is made by Gardner-Gibson of Tampa, Florida), plus the general chemistry of asphalt-emulsion sealers. We have not applied Drive-Maxx ourselves, and where a figure could not be confirmed we say so. The pail you buy is the final word.

blocks.p: All three come in 4.75-gallon pails weighing about 49 lbs, need a 36-hour window free of rain, go onto a slightly damp (not wet) surface, and are not recommended or warranted on slopes steeper than 20 degrees. New asphalt should wait at least six months or a full summer season before its first coat.

sections.h: Is Black Jack Drive-Maxx Any Good?

blocks.p: For a homeowner sealing a residential asphalt driveway, yes. Drive-Maxx sealers are latex-enhanced asphalt emulsions with sand to fill small cracks, the same basic category as the other well-known consumer sealers on the shelf, such as Latex-ite. The directions are detailed and consistent across the range, the recoat times let you finish a two-coat job in one day, and the top-tier 1000 adds a urethane-enhanced, UV-protected film and a cold-weather window few consumer sealers offer.

The catches apply to every product in this aisle. The two-coat requirement means fewer finished square feet per pail than the coverage figure suggests at first glance. The year rating is a maker's claim under ideal conditions, not a resealing schedule. And no sealer fixes structural damage: alligator cracking, potholes or a failing base need repair first, as covered in [how to fix a crumbling asphalt driveway](/how-to-fix-crumbling-asphalt-driveway/). Within those limits, Drive-Maxx is a sound choice, and the real question is which tier.

Drive-Maxx is Black Jack's line of blacktop filler and sealer products. All of them are water-based asphalt emulsions: fine droplets of asphalt suspended in water with clay and fillers. Black Jack adds latex polymers for durability and flexibility: the 500 is described as latex enhanced, the 700 as enhanced with latex, and the 1000 as enhanced with a latex polymer and urethane. Each contains sand to help fill small cracks and give a skid-resistant finish. They are brown in the pail, dry black, clean up with soap and water while wet, and are not coal tar products; see [coal tar vs asphalt emulsion sealer](/coal-tar-vs-asphalt-emulsion-sealer/) for why that matters.

The range has more than three tiers. Black Jack also lists lower tiers below the 500, down to a 2-year pail, and our [Black Jack vs Latex-ite comparison](/black-jack-vs-latex-ite-driveway-sealer/) lays out all five with Black Jack's list prices. Most shoppers compare the 500, 700 and 1000, so that is the focus here.

Black Jack also makes the repair products its sealer sheets tell you to use first: Speed-Fill Elastic Crack Filler for cracks, Speed-Patch for cracks and holes larger than 1 inch, and a permanent pothole patch that needs six weeks to cure before sealing. Our guide to [how long driveway crack filler takes to dry](/how-long-does-driveway-crack-filler-take-to-dry/) covers those waits.

sections.h: What Is the Difference Between Drive-Maxx 500, 700 and 1000?

blocks.p: The number in the name tracks the rated life printed on the pail: 5 years for the 500, 7 for the 700 and 10 for the 1000. Treat these as rankings of durability within the range, not promises. Thin asphalt films wear fastest in tire paths and strong sun, and most homeowners reseal consumer products every two to four years whatever the label says. See [how long driveway sealer lasts](/how-long-does-driveway-sealer-last/).

The 500 is an E-Z stir, latex-enhanced formula with a skid-resistant, rubberized finish. The 700 moves to an advanced gel that Black Jack says spreads faster and more easily, adds a heavy-duty sand mix for traction and keeps the rubberized finish. The 1000 keeps the gel, adds urethane to the latex polymer (which the sheet says delivers the longest life) and adds UV protection so the surface stays black longer.

This is the most important practical difference. The 500 and 700 need 55°F and rising but below 90°F, and the sheets say not to apply if overnight temperatures below 50°F are expected within 36 hours. The 1000 uses what Black Jack calls ClimaSeal technology and can be applied from 45°F to 99°F, with the overnight limit lowered to 45°F. Those ten degrees open up a lot of spring and fall weekends in northern states. See [what temperature to seal a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/).

The 500 and 700 take about 3 to 6 hours before the second coat, 2 to 4 hours to foot traffic and 24 to 48 hours to vehicles. The 1000 cuts the recoat to about 2 to 4 hours and foot traffic to 1 to 2 hours. Black Jack says one hour in good drying conditions, which it defines as above 75°F, clear sunny skies and humidity below 35%, and that vehicles need a minimum of 24 hours. Humid or cloudy weather lengthens all of these.

sections.h: Is Drive-Maxx 1000 Worth the Extra Money?

blocks.p: It is if you need the 45°F window, want to finish a two-coat job in one day, or have a sunny, exposed driveway where UV protection matters. Black Jack calls the 1000 its best-quality rubberized blacktop filler and sealer. The sheet lists a urethane-enhanced latex polymer formula, sand to fill small cracks, UV protection, an advanced gel for easier spreading, Fast Dry (light foot traffic in about an hour in good conditions) and ClimaSeal (cures in cooler temperatures down to 45°F).

Those last two features are what you are really paying for. A wider temperature window means more usable weekends, and the short recoat time means both coats comfortably go down in one day. On a sunny driveway the UV claim should help it stay black longer than the lower tiers, though Black Jack does not publish fade data we could check. The trade-offs: it is the most expensive Drive-Maxx pail, it still needs two coats, vehicles still wait at least 24 hours, and stock varies by store and region.
For a warm-weather job on a driveway you reseal every few years, the 500 or 700 is enough.

sections.h: Drive-Maxx 700 Review: Is the Middle Pail the Sweet Spot?

blocks.p: For a summer job, often yes. Black Jack describes the 700 as a better-quality rubberized blacktop filler and sealer that renews old, worn driveways, with sand to fill small cracks, a heavy-duty sand mix for traction, latex enhancement for durability and a gel for faster, easier installation. Its weather and timing rules match the 500's: 55-90°F, no overnight lows below 50°F for 36 hours, and about 3 to 6 hours between coats.

The step from 500 to 700 buys the gel and the extra sand, which help a beginner spread an even film and leave a slightly more textured, grippy surface. The step from 700 to 1000 buys the colder window, the faster cure and the UV protection. If you seal in July and want something better than the entry tiers, the 700 is the sensible middle.

sections.h: Drive-Maxx 500 Review: Is the Budget Pail Good Enough?

blocks.p: For a warm-weather job on a sound driveway, yes. The 500 is an E-Z stir, latex-enhanced filler and sealer with sand to fill small cracks and a skid-resistant, rubberized finish, rated for 5 years. Its directions match the 700's in every practical respect, so the choice between them comes down to price and whether you want the gel and heavier sand. Because it is a liquid rather than a gel, it is a little easier to over-apply, so keep the coats thin.

It is the right product for a rental, a driveway due for resurfacing in a few years, or anyone who reseals on a short cycle whatever the label says. Questions like will Drive-Maxx 500 dry up almost always come down to weather: apply at 55°F or warmer, keep coats thin and give it the full 24 to 48 hours before driving on it. Our [Black Jack vs Latex-ite comparison](/black-jack-vs-latex-ite-driveway-sealer/) sets the 500 against Latex-ite Airport Grade+.

sections.h: How Many Pails of Drive-Maxx Do You Need?

blocks.p: Because Drive-Maxx needs two coats, one 4.75-gallon pail finishes about half its per-coat figure: roughly 175 square feet on a smooth driveway (350 divided by 2) and 150 on a rough or worn one (300 divided by 2). Porous asphalt that has never been sealed absorbs more of the first coat.

Round up and buy one spare pail for a large or rough driveway; running out halfway through a coat is the quickest way to a patchy finish. When several pails are needed, Black Jack recommends matching batch codes and blending the end of one pail into the start of the next to keep the color even. For a budget, see [how much it costs to seal a driveway](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/).
Black Jack's directions are the same across the 500, 700 and 1000 apart from temperatures and timings:

ol: Check the weather: 55°F and rising but under 90°F for the 500 and 700 (45-99°F for the 1000), and no rain or cold nights for 36 hours.
Turn the pails upside down the night before so settled solids loosen.
Repair first: fill cracks with Speed-Fill, use Speed-Patch for anything over 1 inch, and let repairs cure to their own directions. A permanent pothole patch needs six weeks.
Clean and degrease: pressure-wash the driveway, scrub oil stains with a degreaser or dish soap so the sealer can bond, and rinse.
Remove puddles and apply to a slightly damp, not wet, surface.
Pour about a third of the pail and spread it with a squeegee; Black Jack says a squeegee must be used to get the correct application rate.
Work the whole driveway in one continuous application to avoid color shading, keeping the coat thin.
Apply the second coat perpendicular to the first once the first has cured (about 3-6 hours, or 2-4 for the 1000).
Keep foot traffic off for 2-4 hours (1-2 for the 1000) and vehicles for 24-48 hours.

blocks.p: For a fuller walkthrough including edging and tools, see [how to seal an asphalt driveway](/how-to-seal-an-asphalt-driveway/).

sections.h: What Goes Wrong With Drive-Maxx, and How Do You Avoid It?

ul: Tracking and soft spots: almost always thick coats, cool or humid weather, or driving on it too soon. Two thin coats, the right temperature and the full vehicle wait fix most of it; see [how long driveway sealer takes to dry](/how-long-for-driveway-sealer-to-dry/).
Wash-off: rain inside the 36-hour window can streak or strip a fresh coat. See [rain after sealing a driveway](/rain-after-sealing-driveway/).
Peeling: usually poor prep (dirt, oil, a surface that was too wet or still had puddles) or too many coats built up over the years. See [driveway sealer peeling](/driveway-sealer-peeling/).
Color shading: stopping halfway, or mixing pails from different batches without blending.
Slick or uneven finish on slopes: Black Jack does not warrant Drive-Maxx on slopes over 20 degrees. Work across the slope and keep coats especially thin.

mistakes: Black Jack's sheets say two thin coats are required. One coat may look fine for a few weeks, but it is thinner than the product is designed for and is unlikely to reach its rated life. Budget pails for two coats from the start.
Sealing the 500 or 700 on a cool fall weekend

Both need 55°F and rising with no overnight lows below 50°F for 36 hours. A September afternoon that hits 60°F and drops to 45°F overnight fails that rule; use the 1000, rated to 45°F, or wait for a warmer spell.
The sheets ask for a slightly damp surface, not a wet one. Standing water thins the sealer and leaves weak, pale patches. Rinse, then sweep or blow out puddles before the first pour.
Reading the year number as a reseal date

The 5, 7 and 10 years are rated life under ideal conditions. Most driveways need fresh sealer every two to four years depending on traffic and sun. Reseal when the surface grays, not when the calendar says.
bottomLine: Drive-Maxx is a sound, widely stocked sealer range, and the tiers are easy to read: the number is the rated life, and all three need two thin coats at about 350 square feet per coat. Buy the 1000 for cool-season work, a fast one-day job or a sunny driveway; it is the only tier rated down to 45°F. Buy the 700 for a summer job if you want the gel and extra traction, and the 500 for a rental or a short reseal cycle. Whichever you pick, prep and weather decide more than the tier.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Drive-Maxx 500, 700 and 1000?
faqs.a: The number is the rated life: 5, 7 and 10 years. The 500 is a latex-enhanced E-Z stir formula, the 700 adds a gel and a heavy-duty sand mix, and the 1000 adds urethane, UV protection, a 45-99°F application window (against 55-90°F) and faster recoat and foot-traffic times. All three need two coats at the same coverage.

faqs.q: How long does Drive-Maxx take to dry?
faqs.a: For the 500 and 700, about 3 to 6 hours between coats, 2 to 4 hours to foot traffic and 24 to 48 hours to vehicles. For the 1000, about 2 to 4 hours between coats, 1 to 2 hours to light foot traffic (one hour above 75°F, sunny, under 35% humidity) and at least 24 hours to vehicles. Humid or cloudy weather lengthens all of them.

faqs.q: Is Drive-Maxx 1000 worth the extra money?
faqs.a: It is if you need the 45°F window, want to finish a two-coat job in one day, or have a sunny driveway where UV protection matters. For a warm-weather job on a driveway you reseal every few years, the 500 or 700 is enough, since all three cover the same area per pail.

faqs.q: Can I apply only one coat of Drive-Maxx?
faqs.a: Black Jack's sheets say two thin coats are required. One coat may look fine at first, but it will be thinner than the product is designed for and is unlikely to reach its rated life. Plan on two coats when you count pails.

faqs.q: How long does Drive-Maxx last in the can?
faqs.a: The data sheets say to keep the product from freezing and keep containers closed, but the sheets we read do not print a shelf life. A sealed pail stored indoors above freezing usually stays usable for a season or more. If it has frozen, separated into hard lumps that will not remix, or skinned over heavily, do not use it.

faqs.q: What products are similar to Drive-Maxx 500?
faqs.a: Other water-based, polymer-modified asphalt-emulsion filler sealers in the same price tier, such as Latex-ite Airport Grade+. Compare them on coverage per pail, number of coats and minimum temperature rather than the year rating; our Black Jack vs Latex-ite comparison lines the tiers up.

faqs.q: Can I use Drive-Maxx on a steep driveway?
faqs.a: Black Jack says Drive-Maxx is not recommended or warranted on slopes steeper than 20 degrees. On a moderate slope, work across it, keep both coats thin, and start at the top so excess does not pool at the bottom, where it cures slowly and tracks.
